questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(i) The retreating monsoon is not characterised by:
questions.solution: (d) Heavy rainfall across India. During retreat (Oct-Nov) skies clear and rainfall decreases over most of India; only the Tamil Nadu coast gets heavy rain.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(ii) Which of the following is a transported soil?
questions.solution: (d) Alluvial soil. Alluvial soil is deposited by rivers (transported); the others are formed in situ.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(iii) Chir pine is a type of vegetation found at an altitude between -
questions.solution: (a) 1500m and 1750m. Between 1500 and 1750 m in the Himalayas pine forests are well developed, with Chir pine as a useful commercial tree.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(iv) Tanks form the main source of irrigation in -
questions.solution: (b) The Deccan Plateau. The undulating, hard-rock Deccan Plateau has natural depressions and impermeable rock, ideal for tanks.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(v) The main buyers of Indian manganese are -
questions.solution: (c) Japan and West Germany. Japan and (West) Germany have been the main importers of Indian manganese ore for their steel industries.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(vi) Which of the following is not a feature of mixed farming?

options.a: Crops and animals are raised simultaneously
options.b: Rotation of crops is not practiced
options.c: Two or more crops are grown together
options.d: Ensures steady income to the farmers.

questions.solution: (b) Rotation of crops is not practiced. Mixed farming does practise crop rotation; the other three are its features.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(vii) India has a world monopoly of ___ produced in Assam.
questions.solution: (c) Yellow muga silk. Golden-yellow Muga silk is produced only in Assam.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(viii) The Ahmedabad-Vadodara region is famous for-
questions.solution: (b) Cotton textile. The region grew around the cotton textile industry (cotton belt, humid climate, Ahmedabad mills).

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(ix) India's first 6-lane concrete, high speed, tolled expressway is -
questions.solution: (c) Mumbai-Pune Expressway. The Mumbai-Pune Expressway (opened 2002) was India's first 6-lane concrete, access-controlled tolled expressway.

questions.question:
Choose the correct options to the questions given below:
(x) Assertion (A): Open Dumping is not environment friendly.
Reason (R): The burning of waste materials in the open dumps pollutes the air.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.c: A is true but R is false
options.d: A is false but R is true.

questions.solution: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Open dumps are burnt, releasing smoke and toxic gases - this air pollution is why open dumping is not environment friendly.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
With reference to the pressure condition prevailing in the North East Monsoon season, answer the following questions:
(a) What kind of wind prevails over the country during this season?
(b) What is the weather characterized by in this season in terms of pressure?
questions.solution: (a) Cold, dry North-East (offshore) trade/monsoon winds blowing from land to sea prevail. (b) High pressure develops over the north-western plains and Central Asia (cold land), so the weather is cool, dry and clear with low pressure over the seas.

marking_points.point: (a) Cold, dry NE winds blowing from land to sea
(b) High pressure over the land (NW India) - cool, clear, dry weather

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Answer the following:
(a) What are Jet Streams?
(b) How do the easterly jet streams influence the climate of India?
questions.solution: (a) Jet streams are fast-moving, narrow belts of westerly/easterly winds blowing in the upper troposphere (about 9-12 km above the surface). (b) In summer the tropical easterly jet stream blows over peninsular India (about 15°N); it helps in the sudden onset/burst of the south-west monsoon and influences tropical depressions that bring rain.

marking_points.point: (a) Definition - high-velocity narrow upper-air wind belts
(b) Easterly jet helps sudden burst/onset of SW monsoon and rainfall

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for each of the following:
(a) Jammu and Kashmir is affected by western disturbances.
(b) The month of October is marked by sultry humid weather.
(c) Temperate cyclones from Mediterranean Sea in winter are beneficial in Delhi, Haryana, Punjab and western Uttar Pradesh.
questions.solution: (a) In winter the westerly jet stream brings temperate cyclones (western disturbances) from the Mediterranean Sea; they enter India from the north-west and first strike Jammu and Kashmir, bringing snowfall/rain. (b) In October the monsoon retreats; skies clear and temperatures rise while the land is still moist, so high temperature with high humidity creates oppressive 'October heat'. (c) They bring light winter rainfall which is very beneficial for the rabi crops, especially wheat, grown in these states.

marking_points.point: (a) Western disturbances from Mediterranean enter from NW, first reach J&K
(b) Retreating monsoon - clear skies, high temp + moist land = humidity (October heat)
(c) Winter rain benefits rabi crops like wheat

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Study the data of distribution of temperature and rainfall for the station and answer the questions that follow:
Months: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
Temperature (°C): 15.4 19.5 24.9 29.6 31.5 31.7 30 29.8 29.2 27.1 22.3 17.2
Rainfall (mm): 11 14 10 13 45 165 355 280 200 50 7 6
(a) Calculate the annual rainfall experienced by the station.
(b) Name the season where the rainfall is the highest.
(c) Calculate the average annual range of temperature of the station.
questions.solution: (a) Annual rainfall = 11+14+10+13+45+165+355+280+200+50+7+6 = 1156 mm. (b) The rainy season / South-West monsoon season (June-September, maximum in July). (c) Annual range = highest - lowest = 31.7°C (June) - 15.4°C (January) = 16.3°C.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Your brother lives in a hilly terrain that receives heavy rainfall and grows crops like tea, coffee, tapioca and cashew nuts.
(a) What type of soil is available in the said area?
(b) How is it formed?
questions.solution: (a) Laterite soil. (b) It is formed under high temperature and heavy rainfall with alternate wet and dry seasons; intense leaching washes away silica and lime, leaving behind oxides of iron and aluminium.

marking_points.point: (b) Leaching under heavy rain/high temp removes silica & lime, leaving iron and aluminium oxides

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.topic: Regur soil, soil conservation, erosion causes
questions.question:
Answer very briefly:
(a) Name two states in India where Regur soil is found.
(b) What is soil conservation?
(c) Give two man-made causes of soil erosion.
questions.solution: (a) Maharashtra and Gujarat (also Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana). (b) Soil conservation is the protection of soil from erosion and loss of fertility by suitable methods such as afforestation, contour ploughing, terracing and checking overgrazing. (c) Deforestation and overgrazing (also faulty farming methods like ploughing along slopes, shifting cultivation, mining).

marking_points.point: (b) Definition - protecting soil from erosion and maintaining fertility
(c) Two man-made causes e.g. deforestation, overgrazing

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for the following:
(a) Agricultural lands are getting transformed into ravines in Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.
(b) Wind erosion reduces the productive capacity of the soil.
(c) Khadar is the younger alluvium.
questions.solution: (a) Heavy rainfall on soft alluvial soil with sparse vegetation (Chambal valley) causes gully erosion; the gullies deepen and widen into ravines, making land unfit for cultivation. (b) Wind blows away the fertile, fine top soil particles, leaving behind coarse sand and reducing fertility. (c) Khadar is newly deposited alluvium laid down every year by floods in the flood plains of rivers, hence it is younger (unlike older bhangar).

marking_points.point: (a) Gully erosion of soft soil develops into ravines
(c) Deposited annually by floods in flood plains - new alluvium

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Give two points of difference between Agro forestry and Traditional forestry.
questions.solution: 1. Agro-forestry is the growing of trees together with crops and/or livestock on the same farm land, whereas traditional forestry is the growing/managing of trees alone on forest land. 2. Agro-forestry is practised by farmers to meet needs of fuel, fodder, fruit and income alongside food crops, whereas traditional forestry mainly aims at producing timber and forest products and is managed largely by the Forest Department.

marking_points.point: Difference 1 (trees with crops on farmland vs trees alone on forest land)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: State two characteristics of tropical desert vegetation with one example of its species.
questions.solution: Characteristics: 1. Plants are xerophytic - thorny bushes and scrubs with long roots to reach underground water. 2. Leaves are small/thick or modified into spines and stems are fleshy to reduce transpiration. Example: babul, kikar, khair, cactus, khejri or date palm.

marking_points.point: Two characteristics (xerophytic, long roots, spines/thick leaves)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give geographical reason for each of the following:
(a) Protection of natural vegetation is crucial.
(b) Dry deciduous forests look like a vast grassland with naked trees.
(c) Tropical rainforests do not support the growth of herbs and grasses.
questions.solution: (a) Natural vegetation maintains ecological balance, prevents soil erosion and floods, provides habitat to wildlife and supplies timber, fuel and other products - so it must be protected. (b) In the long dry season trees shed their leaves to conserve water, so the area appears as grassland with leafless (naked) trees. (c) The dense, multi-layered canopy of tall evergreen trees prevents sunlight from reaching the ground, so herbs and grasses cannot grow.

marking_points.point: (b) Trees shed leaves in long dry season

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Answer very briefly.
(a) State one regulatory function of forests.
(b) Name two Tropical Moist Deciduous Forest species.
(c) Mention one objective of Van Mahotsav.
questions.solution: (a) Forests regulate the climate / water cycle - they increase humidity, control floods and maintain the oxygen-carbon dioxide balance. (b) Teak and sal (also sandalwood, shisham, mahua). (c) To create awareness about the importance of trees and encourage large-scale planting of trees (every July).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: State two points of differences between traditional and modern means of irrigation.
questions.solution: 1. Traditional means (wells, tanks, inundation canals) use simple, locally-made devices and animal/human power, whereas modern means (tube wells, perennial canals, sprinkler, drip) use electric/diesel pumps and modern technology. 2. Traditional means waste more water and irrigate small areas; modern means are efficient, conserve water and irrigate larger areas throughout the year.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Ravi has installed a system of long hose that is set to a water source on one side and water is released on the other side through guns to the field.
(a) What type of irrigation is being described above?
(b) Mention one disadvantage of the same.
questions.solution: (a) Sprinkler irrigation. (b) It has a high initial cost (needs pipes, pumps, nozzles and power) / water is lost by evaporation and wind drift in hot, windy weather.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
'Terrain of Deccan Plateau is uneven with many natural depressions.'
(a) What sort of irrigation is suitable in the above terrain?
(b) Give two advantages to this type of irrigation.
questions.solution: (a) Tank irrigation. (b) 1. Tanks are cheap to build - natural depressions only need an earthen bund, and they have a long life. 2. Rain water is stored in the rainy season and can be used in the dry season; tanks can also be used for fishing.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for the following:
(a) Tubewell irrigation is expensive.
(b) Well irrigation is confined to the alluvial plains.
(c) Runoff from paved surfaces is used for storing of water.
questions.solution: (a) Tube wells need deep boring, costly electric/diesel pumps and regular supply of electricity, and the water table keeps falling. (b) Alluvial soil is soft and porous, so digging is easy and the water table is high with plenty of groundwater. (c) Paved surfaces do not let water seep in; collecting this runoff (rainwater harvesting) conserves water and recharges groundwater instead of letting it go waste.

marking_points.point: (a) High cost of boring, pumps, electricity

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
'In nature copper occurs in the native form and in three principal combinations.'
(a) Name the three principal combinations.
(b) Write two uses of copper.
questions.solution: (a) Sulphides, oxides and carbonates. (b) Electrical wires and cables / electrical goods (good conductor); making alloys like brass and bronze, utensils and coins.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Coal can be classified into Anthracite, Bituminous, Lignite and Peat.
(a) What are the bases on which the above classification is made?
(b) Mention the types of coal fields found in India.
questions.solution: (a) On the basis of carbon content (and hence heat/calorific value) and the moisture/volatile matter present. (b) Gondwana coalfields (about 250 million years old, e.g. Damodar valley - Jharia, Raniganj) and Tertiary coalfields (younger, e.g. Assam, Meghalaya, Jammu and Kashmir; lignite at Neyveli).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Carefully study the picture and answer the following questions:
[Picture: photograph of a large concrete dam with many sluice gates, captioned 'HIRAKUD DAM - India's largest dam'.]
(a) On which river is the dam built?
(b) Mention the districts that benefit from this particular dam and how?
questions.solution: (a) The Hirakud dam is built on the river Mahanadi (near Sambalpur, Odisha). (b) Districts of Sambalpur, Bargarh, Bolangir and Subarnapur (Sonepur) benefit - it provides irrigation through canals, hydroelectricity, and controls floods in the Mahanadi delta (Cuttack, Puri).

marking_points.point: (b) Benefits: irrigation, hydel power, flood control

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
State the following:
(a) Distribution of Natural Gas
(b) Two nuclear power stations with states in India.
(c) 'Tidal energy is easy to harness'. How?
questions.solution: (a) Natural gas is found in Mumbai High and Bassein (offshore, Arabian Sea), the Krishna-Godavari basin (Andhra Pradesh), Gujarat (Ankleshwar, Cambay), Assam and Tripura, and Rajasthan (Jaisalmer). (b) Tarapur - Maharashtra; Kudankulam - Tamil Nadu (also Rawatbhata - Rajasthan, Narora - UP, Kaiga - Karnataka, Kakrapar - Gujarat). (c) Tides rise and fall twice daily in a regular, predictable way; water entering a narrow gulf/estuary at high tide can be trapped behind a dam and released through turbines at low tide - e.g. Gulf of Kutch and Gulf of Khambhat with high tidal range.

marking_points.point: (c) Regular predictable tides trapped in gulfs/estuaries to run turbines

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
'New canes are usually planted by taking cuttings from old plants.'
(a) Identify the method of cultivation from the above description.
(b) Name the perennial crop that is cultivated through the identified method.
questions.solution: (a) Ratooning (vegetative propagation by cuttings/setts from old plants). (b) Sugarcane.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
It is referred to as 'golden fibre' as it provides huge revenue to the government.
(a) Which crop is referred to as the golden fibre?
(b) Name the inferior substitute for the same crop.
questions.solution: (a) Jute (b) Mesta

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
State the following:
(a) Any two problems of sugarcane cultivators.
(b) The leading producer of Groundnut.
questions.solution: (a) 1. Low yield per hectare due to small holdings and poor irrigation/inputs. 2. Delayed payment and low prices from sugar mills; high cost of cultivation and pests/diseases. (b) Gujarat is the leading producer of groundnut in India.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for each of the following:
(a) Mustard is widely grown in Sutlej-Ganga Plain.
(b) The coffee plantation is interspersed with trees of silver oak and jackfruit.
(c) Intensive farming is practiced in high density population areas.
questions.solution: (a) Mustard is a rabi crop needing cool climate, light rain/irrigation and loamy alluvial soil - all available in the Sutlej-Ganga plain; winter rain from western disturbances also helps. (b) Coffee plants need shade from direct sunlight; silver oak and jackfruit trees provide shade (and extra income). (c) Land per person is small, so farmers use high inputs (HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation, labour) and multiple cropping to get maximum yield from the limited land to feed the large population.

marking_points.point: (a) Cool winter climate, alluvial soil, irrigation
(c) Small holdings - maximise output to feed many

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Briefly explain the Chota Nagpur Plateau Region as a major industrial region. (Write in points)
questions.solution: 1. Rich deposits of coal (Jharia, Bokaro) and iron ore, manganese, limestone close by - ideal for heavy industry. 2. Hydro and thermal power from the Damodar Valley Corporation; cheap labour from nearby states and nearness to Kolkata port. Hence major iron and steel plants at Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Durgapur and heavy engineering at Ranchi.

marking_points.point: Availability of raw materials (coal, iron ore)
Power, labour/market/port and named steel centres

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: 'Mumbai is rightly called the cottonpolis of India'. Give four reasons why it is called so.
questions.solution: 1. Humid coastal climate prevents the yarn from breaking. 2. Port facilities to import machinery and long-staple cotton and export finished cloth. 3. Nearness to the cotton-growing black soil areas of Maharashtra and Gujarat, with good rail/road links. 4. Availability of capital, cheap skilled labour, power (Tata hydel) and a large market; it had the largest number of cotton mills.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for the following:
(a) The Government of India is promoting and planning to set up more mini steel plants.
(b) Bengaluru and Hyderabad are leading centres of software industries.
(c) The cotton industry faces constant threat of sickness and consequent closure.
questions.solution: (a) Mini steel plants need less capital and time to build, use scrap iron and sponge iron with electric furnaces, can be set up near markets and produce special/alloy steel. (b) They have many technical and research institutes providing skilled IT professionals, good infrastructure, pleasant climate and government support (software technology parks). (c) Mills use old, obsolete machinery, face shortage of good long-staple cotton, power cuts, labour problems and stiff competition from powerlooms and synthetic fibres.

marking_points.point: (a) Low cost, use scrap, decentralised, alloy steel

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Since its inception, the Make In India Programme has been pivotal in elevating India in the global manufacturing landscape. Presently, the Make In India 2.0 initiative spans as many as 27 parts of the economy and it is clear that there have been significant accomplishments more vigorous than before, further consolidating India's role in the global manufacturing ecosystem. - Hindustan Times, 13.10.25
(a) When was the above stated scheme launched?
(b) What are its four pillars?
questions.solution: (a) Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014. (b) Four pillars: New Processes, New Infrastructure, New Sectors and New Mindset.

marking_points.point: (b) Four pillars: new processes, new infrastructure, new sectors, new mindset

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Mention two major projects undertaken by the National Highway Authority of India.
(b) State the major difference between a Highway and an Expressway.
questions.solution: (a) The Golden Quadrilateral (linking Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata) and the North-South and East-West Corridors (also Bharatmala Pariyojana). (b) An expressway is a high-speed, access-controlled road (vehicles enter/exit only at fixed points, no crossings, usually tolled), whereas a highway is not access-controlled and has intersections and slower mixed traffic.

marking_points.point: (b) Expressway is access-controlled high-speed road; highway is not

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Give any two disadvantages of Railways Transport.
questions.solution: 1. Construction and maintenance of tracks is very costly and difficult in hilly, forested and desert regions. 2. Railways cannot provide door-to-door service (inflexible routes and timings); different gauges cause trans-shipment delays.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for the following:
(a) Air transport is of particular significance during natural calamities.
(b) River Ganga is navigable from its mouth right up to Allahabad.
(c) Broad gauge is also called India gauge.
questions.solution: (a) When roads and railways are destroyed by floods, earthquakes or landslides, aircraft/helicopters can quickly reach inaccessible areas to drop relief and evacuate people. (b) It is a perennial river fed by Himalayan snow, flowing over a gentle-sloped plain with enough depth of water and no waterfalls/rapids up to Prayagraj (Allahabad). (c) Broad gauge (1.676 m) is the standard gauge adopted for India's main network and is unique to the Indian subcontinent, hence called India gauge.

marking_points.point: (a) Reaches inaccessible areas quickly for relief
(c) Main/unique gauge of Indian railways (1.676 m)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) State the connectivity of National Waterway No. 1 (NW-1). Mention its objective.
(b) Name India's first semi-high speed fully air conditioned train introduced by Indian Railways and when.
questions.solution: (a) NW-1 runs on the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system from Prayagraj (Allahabad) to Haldia (about 1620 km). Objective: to provide cheap, fuel-efficient, eco-friendly transport of bulk cargo and reduce load on road/rail. (b) Vande Bharat Express (Train 18), introduced in February 2019 (New Delhi-Varanasi).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Define:
(a) Eutrophication.
(b) Biomagnification.
questions.solution: (a) Eutrophication is the excessive enrichment of a water body with nutrients (nitrates, phosphates from fertilisers/sewage), causing algal bloom that depletes dissolved oxygen and kills aquatic life. (b) Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of non-biodegradable toxic substances (e.g. DDT, mercury) at each successive level of a food chain.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: State one cause of water pollution. Name two common bacterial water borne diseases.
questions.solution: Cause: discharge of untreated sewage / industrial effluents into rivers (or fertiliser runoff). Bacterial water-borne diseases: cholera and typhoid (also bacillary dysentery).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
'E-waste is valuable as a source for secondary raw material but hazardous if treated and discarded improperly.'
(a) What is E-waste or electronic waste?
(b) Name any two toxic substances present in electronic waste that makes it hazardous.
(c) Why is electronic waste difficult to recycle?
questions.solution: (a) E-waste is discarded, broken or obsolete electrical and electronic equipment such as computers, mobile phones, TVs and refrigerators. (b) Lead and mercury (also cadmium, arsenic, beryllium, brominated flame retardants). (c) It contains a complex mixture of many materials (metals, plastics, glass) fused together in small quantities, so dismantling and separating them is difficult, costly and hazardous without special technology.

marking_points.point: (c) Complex mixture of materials - hard/costly/hazardous to separate

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Carefully study the picture and answer the following questions:
[Picture titled 'The changing face of Taj Mahal' showing the monument THEN (white) and NOW (yellowed/discoloured).]
(a) What could be the possible cause of the changing face of the Taj Mahal?
(b) How does it affect human health and plant life? (Write in points)
questions.solution: (a) Air pollution and acid rain - sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from the Mathura refinery, industries and vehicles combine with rain water to form acids that corrode the marble (marble cancer), along with deposition of soot/particulate matter that yellows it. (b) Human health: polluted air causes respiratory problems like asthma and bronchitis and irritation of eyes/skin. Plant life: acid rain damages leaves, leaches nutrients from soil and reduces growth/kills plants.

marking_points.point: (a) Air pollution / acid rain (SO2, NOx) corroding marble
